3: Wherefore forsakest thou the lovely maiden, That in the dance so sweetly sang?
10: Ah! in the midst of it there sprang A red mouse from her mouth—sufficient reason.
17: That’s nothing! One must not so squeamish be; So the mouse was not gray, enough for thee. Who’d think of that in love’s selected season?
29: Mephisto, seest thou there, Alone and far, a girl most pale and fair? She falters on, her way scarce knowing, As if with fettered feet that stay her going. I must confess, it seems to me As if my kindly Margaret were she.
37: Let the thing be! All thence have evil drawn: It is a magic shape, a lifeless eidolon. Such to encounter is not good: Their blank, set stare benumbs the human blood, And one is almost turned to stone. Medusa’s tale to thee is known.
47: Forsooth, the eyes they are of one whom, dying, No hand with loving pressure closed; That is the breast whereon I once was lying,— The body sweet, beside which I reposed!
54: Tis magic all, thou fool, seduced so easily! Unto each man his love she seems to be.
60:
The woe, the rapture, so ensnare me, That from her gaze I cannot tear me! And, strange! around her fairest throat A single scarlet band is gleaming, No broader than a knife-blade seeming!

Quite right! The mark I also note. Her head beneath her arm she’ll sometimes carry; Twas Perseus lopped it, her old adversary. Thou crav’st the same illusion still! Come, let us mount this little hill; The Prater shows no livelier stir, And, if they’ve not bewitched my sense, I verily see a theatre. What’s going on?
68: SERVIBILIS ’Twill shortly recommence: A new performance—’tis the last of seven. To give that number is the custom here: ’Twas by a Dilettante written, And Dilettanti in the parts appear. That now I vanish, pardon, I entreat you! As Dilettante I the curtain raise.
74: MEPHISTOPHELES When I upon the Blocksberg meet you, I find it good: for that’s your proper place.
89: Sons of Mieding, rest to-day! Needless your machinery: Misty vale and mountain gray, That is all the scenery.
96: That the wedding golden be. Must fifty years be rounded: But the Golden give to me, When the strife’s compounded.
103: Spirits, if you’re here, be seen— Show yourselves, delighted! Fairy king and fairy queen, They are newly plighted.
109: Cometh Puck, and, light of limb, Whisks and whirls in measure: Come a hundred after him, To share with him the pleasure.
116: Ariel’s song is heavenly-pure, His tones are sweet and rare ones: Though ugly faces he allure, Yet he allures the fair ones.
123: Spouses, who would fain agree, Learn how we were mated! If your pairs would loving be, First be separated!
130: If her whims the wife control, And the man berate her, Take him to the Northern Pole, And her to the Equator!
138: Snout of fly, mosquito-bill, And kin of all conditions, Frog in grass, and cricket-trill,— These are the musicians!
145: See the bagpipe on our track! ’Tis the soap-blown bubble: Hear the schnecke-schnicke-schnack Through his nostrils double!
153: Spider’s foot and paunch of toad, And little wings—we know ’em! A little creature ’twill not be, But yet, a little poem.
160: Little step and lofty leap Through honey-dew and fragrance: You’ll never mount the airy steep With all your tripping vagrance.
167: Is’t but masquerading play? See I with precision? Oberon, the beauteous fay, Meets, to-night, my vision!
174: Not a claw, no tail I see! And yet, beyond a cavil, Like “the Gods of Greece,” must he Also be a devil.
182: I only seize, with sketchy air, Some outlines of the tourney; Yet I betimes myself prepare For my Italian journey.
189: My bad luck brings me here, alas! How roars the orgy louder! And of the witches in the mass, But only two wear powder.
196: Powder becomes, like petticoat, A gray and wrinkled noddy; So I sit naked on my goat, And show a strapping body.
202: We’ve too much tact and policy To rate with gibes a scolder; Yet, young and tender though you be, I hope to see you moulder.
209: Fly-snout and mosquito-bill, Don’t swarm so round the Naked! Frog in grass and cricket-trill, Observe the time, and make it!
221: Society to one’s desire! Brides only, and the sweetest! And bachelors of youth and fire. And prospects the completest!
233: And if the Earth don’t open now To swallow up each ranter, Why, then will I myself, I vow, Jump into hell instanter!
239: Us as little insects see! With sharpest nippers flitting, That our Papa Satan we May honor as is fitting.
246: How, in crowds together massed, They are jesting, shameless! They will even say, at last, That their hearts are blameless.
252: Among this witches’ revelry His way one gladly loses; And, truly, it would easier be Than to command the Muses.
262: The proper folks one’s talents laud: Come on, and none shall pass us! The Blocksberg has a summit broad, Like Germany’s Parnassus.
276: Say, who’s the stiff and pompous man? He walks with haughty paces: He snuffles all he snuffle can: “He scents the Jesuits’ traces.”
283: Both clear and muddy streams, for me Are good to fish and sport in: And thus the pious man you see With even devils consorting.
290: Yes, for the pious, I suspect, All instruments are fitting; And on the Blocksberg they erect Full many a place of meeting.
297: A newer chorus now succeeds! I hear the distant drumming. “Don’t be disturbed! ’tis, in the reeds, The bittern’s changeless booming.”
304: How each his legs in nimble trip Lifts up, and makes a clearance! The crooked jump, the heavy skip, Nor care for the appearance.
311: The rabble by such hate are held, To maim and slay delights them: As Orpheus’ lyre the brutes compelled, The bagpipe here unites them.
318: I’ll not be led by any lure Of doubts or critic-cavils: The Devil must be something, sure,— Or how should there be devils?
325: This once, the fancy wrought in me Is really too despotic: Forsooth, if I am all I see, I must be idiotic!
332: This racking fuss on every hand, It gives me great vexation; And, for the first time, here I stand On insecure foundation.
339: With much delight I see the play, And grant to these their merits, Since from the devils I also may Infer the better spirits.
346: The flame they follow, on and on, And think they’re near the treasure: But Devil rhymes with Doubt alone, So I am here with pleasure.
353: Frog in green, and cricket-trill. Such dilettants!—perdition! Fly-snout and mosquito-bill,— Each one’s a fine musician!
360: Sans souci, we call the clan Of merry creatures so, then; Go a-foot no more we can, And on our heads we go, then.
367: Once many a bit we sponged, but now, God help us! that is done with: Our shoes are all danced out, we trow, We’ve but naked soles to run with.
374: From the marshes we appear, Where we originated; Yet in the ranks, at once, we’re here As glittering gallants rated.
382: Darting hither from the sky, In star and fire light shooting, Cross-wise now in grass I lie: Who’ll help me to my footing?
395: Room! and round about us, room! Trodden are the grasses: Spirits also, spirits come, And they are bulky masses.
402: Enter not so stall-fed quite, Like elephant-calves about one! And the heaviest weight to-night Be Puck, himself, the stout one!
409: If loving Nature at your back, Or Mind, the wings uncloses, Follow up my airy track To the mount of roses!
418:
pianissimo Cloud and trailing mist o’erhead Are now illuminated: Air in leaves, and wind in reed, And all is dissipated.

In misery! In despair! Long wretchedly astray on the face of the earth, and now imprisoned! That gracious, ill-starred creature shut in a dungeon as a criminal, and given up to fearful torments! To this has it come! to this!—Treacherous, contemptible spirit, and thou hast concealed it from me!—Stand, then,—stand! Roll the devilish eyes wrathfully in thy head! Stand and defy me with thine intolerable presence! Imprisoned! In irretrievable misery! Delivered up to evil spirits, and to condemning, unfeeling Man! And thou hast lulled me, meanwhile, with the most insipid dissipations, hast concealed from me her increasing wretchedness, and suffered her to go helplessly to ruin!
434:
She is not the first.

Dog! Abominable monster! Transform him, thou Infinite Spirit! transform the reptile again into his dog-shape? in which it pleased him often at night to scamper on before me, to roll himself at the feet of the unsuspecting wanderer, and hang upon his shoulders when he fell! Transform him again into his favorite likeness, that he may crawl upon his belly in the dust before me,—that I may trample him, the outlawed, under foot! Not the first! O woe! woe which no human soul can grasp, that more than one being should sink into the depths of this misery,—that the first, in its writhing death-agony under the eyes of the Eternal Forgiver, did not expiate the guilt of all others! The misery of this single one pierces to the very marrow of my life; and thou art calmly grinning at the fate of thousands!
440: Now we are already again at the end of our wits, where the understanding of you men runs wild. Why didst thou enter into fellowship with us, if thou canst not carry it out? Wilt fly, and art not secure against dizziness? Did we thrust ourselves upon thee, or thou thyself upon us?
449: Gnash not thus thy devouring teeth at me? It fills me with horrible disgust. Mighty, glorious Spirit, who hast vouchsafed to me Thine apparition, who knowest my heart and my soul, why fetter me to the felon-comrade, who feeds on mischief and gluts himself with ruin?
458: Rescue her, or woe to thee! The fearfullest curse be upon thee for thousands of ages!
466: I cannot loosen the bonds of the Avenger, nor undo his bolts. Rescue her? Who was it that plunged her into ruin? I, or thou?
475: Wilt thou grasp the thunder? Well that it has not been given to you, miserable mortals! To crush to pieces the innocent respondent—that is the tyrant-fashion of relieving one’s self in embarrassments.
482: Take me thither! She shall be free!
493: And the danger to which thou wilt expose thyself? Know that the guilt of blood, from thy hand, still lies upon the town! Avenging spirits hover over the spot where the victim fell, and lie in wait for the returning murderer.
500:
That, too, from thee? Murder and death of a world upon thee, monster! Take me thither, I say, and liberate her!

I will convey thee there; and hear, what I can do! Have I all the power in Heaven and on Earth? I will becloud the jailer’s senses: get possession of the key, and lead her forth with human hand! I will keep watch: the magic steeds are ready, I will carry you off. So much is in my power.
519: (FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES speeding onward on black horses.)
527: What weave they there round the raven-stone?
532: I know not what they are brewing and doing.
